title: Chapter 175 – The Long Run Home
html:
[The Mother Tree Orchard – Lin Jian]

The root-hall ends in a door of living wood, and Lin Jian pushes it open with the flat of his staff and steps out into the end of the world.

It is morning. He knows this only because the light is gray and thin and comes from the wrong side of the sky. The orchard is gone. Where the old terraces once ran in neat green steps down the hill, there is a field of turned earth and splintered trunks, torn open from below as if a great hand had thrust up through the soil and left the wreckage where it fell. The air tastes of iron and smoke. Somewhere to the north, very far, a horn is blowing.

He stands under the Mother Tree and does not move.

It is enormous. He has known this for months, in the way a man knows the size of a mountain from a map. He did not know it in his body. The trunk rises beside him like the wall of a city, wrinkled and silver-barked, and its crown spreads across half the sky in a dome of pale leaves that glow faintly from within. A hundred feet up, the leaves are quiet. Around the base, in a ring thirty paces wide, the ground is clear. Nothing lies there. Not a broken branch. Not a bone.

Outside the ring, the dead lie in drifts.

Crawlers, he thinks. Hundreds. Pale bodies, curled and broken, piled against the line where the tree's reach ends as against a wall. Some are still twitching. The roots have taken most of them. A few still thrash in the soil, held by white tendrils as fine as thread.

He leans on the staff. His chest is a bellows with a hole in it. He coughs, and tastes copper, and wipes his mouth on the back of his hand without looking.

He reads it once, with a flat tired eye, and lets the panel fade.

Do not run, he thinks. Eleven miles. Through that.

Behind him, in the root-hall, under sixteen hours of stone, a man named Kito spent himself so that he could stand here. He will not be walking out again.

Jian shuts his eyes for a breath.

When he opens them, a root is lying across his boot.

It is thin and white, no thicker than a finger, and it has come out of the bark at the height of his knee without a sound. It does not grip. It rests, as a hand rests on a sleeve, and it is warm. Slowly, at the end, a bead of pale sap swells and hangs from its tip like a drop of milk.

The lullaby is very close here. It is not a sound so much as a pressure behind the eyes, a slow patient rocking, and he knows the voice now. He has heard it in his own head for months and taken it for memory. It is Mei's. It is a child of eleven years, in a hospital bed in another world, humming to herself in the dark to keep from being afraid, and it has been going out through a stored pattern and a tree for longer than he has been alive.

"I can't stay," he says aloud. His voice is a rasp. "I'm sorry. I have to reach the Wall."

The bead of sap trembles.

Take it, the hum seems to say. Please.

He should not. Every gift in his life has had a hook in it, and this one is a gift from a child who cannot count what she gives. But eleven miles stand between him and the people he loves, and his lungs are full of knives, so he bends, with a grunt, and touches his tongue to the bead.

It tastes of rain on warm stone. Heat runs down his throat and spreads under his ribs, and the knives in his chest go soft. His next breath is the first clean one in a month. He stands up straighter than he has stood since spring.

He stares at the panel. Then he lowers his head against the bark, once, briefly, and says to the tree, to the child inside it, to the whole long strange machine of mercy and theft that has made him: "Thank you. I'll be quick."

The root slides off his boot and goes back into the wood.

He tightens his grip on the staff, and starts down the hill.

* * *

The first mile is a slaughterhouse, and he walks it.

He does not run. Not yet. The Core Step is a fold, and a fold costs gold: a thin dry scratch of wear along the Core each time, like a file on a lock, and he has only so many. He spends none of it on the open ground. He picks his way down the broken terraces with the staff and the black ash of the orchard under his boots, and the dead crawlers lie on both sides of the path, and the living ones flow past him.

They flow past. That is the strange thing. Twice a pale shape comes at him out of the smoke, and twice it veers at ten paces, as if it had remembered something. A Gnasher the size of a cart lumbers through the wreckage of a pear terrace, turns its blind face toward him, and stops. It stands there for the space of three breaths with its jaws half open. Then it goes on, heavily, toward the tree.

It does not want me, he realizes. It wants what I came out of.

The thought is cold and exact. He has come up from the root-hall with something inside his cloak that the beasts can smell: Kito's fold, still ringing in his bones, the Seventh Door's breath. The beasts are drawn to the tree as iron to a lodestone. He is only a stone on the road between.

He keeps walking.

At the bottom of the third terrace he finds the first human body. A Garden guard in a quilted gown, lying on her back with her spear in her hands and her eyes open. There is no wound on her that he can see. Her face is peaceful, and gray, and very young. He crouches, with an effort that makes his knees crack, and lays two fingers on her throat.

Nothing.

He closes her eyes. He puts her spear across her chest, the way the pupils do it, and he says her name, because he has read it on her sleeve: Tess. And then he stands up, and goes on.

He does not look at the next one.

* * *

At the old well-house, he finds the first living man.

The building has half fallen in. Its roof beams stick up through the thatch like broken ribs, and in the doorway, propped against the stone with a crossbow across his knees, sits a Garden guard with a bandage round his head. He sees Jian coming through the smoke, and does not seem to believe it.

"Young Master," he says hoarsely. And then, as the shape resolves, a little louder: "Lin Jian. By the Founders."

"Stay seated." Jian crosses the yard. He kneels, with difficulty, and looks at the bandage. It is soaked through. "How long?"

"Since dusk." The man tries a laugh and it turns into a cough. "They came up under the pear rows. We never heard them. Clan Head Zhao pulled everyone back to the Wall at the first bell, but a few of us were out in the lower rows and the way was cut. Four of us made it here." He jerks his head at the dark behind him. "Two are still in there. I think the little one's dead."

Jian looks. In the shadow of the fallen beam, a girl of perhaps seventeen is curled around a bundle of cloth. Her chest is rising. Beside her, a boy lies very still.

"The Wall is eleven miles," says the guard. "You can't get to it."

"It is eight, by the lower road."

"Eight, then. Through that." The man looks at the staff, at the black stains on Jian's cuffs, at the gray in his hair. His face changes. "You've been sick, haven't you? Everybody says."

"Yes."

"Then you shouldn't—" He stops. Something in Jian's face has stopped him.

"I have a little time," Jian says. "I would like to spend it getting there."

He takes a black wax pill from the pouch at his belt, one of Bell's, and holds it out. The man looks at it, then at him.

"For the bleeding," says Jian. "Chew it. Don't swallow. Then stay here until someone comes."

"Who will come?"

"Someone."

Before he goes, he does one more thing. He walks into the ruin, shoulders a fallen beam off the girl and the boy, and carries the bundle of cloth to the cellar stair, where the stone still stands and the door still holds. The girl follows, blinking. She is seventeen. Her name is Sun. She has a cut over one eye and has not stopped trembling since dusk.

"The boy," she says. "Is he—"

Jian puts two fingers on the boy's throat. There is a pulse there, faint and fluttering. "He lives. Keep him warm. Do not open the cellar door until you hear the horn blown twice, and then once."

"Twice, then once."

"If you do not hear it by tomorrow's dusk, go north, to the Wall. Do not wait for anyone."

She nods. She is crying without a sound, the way the very young cry when they have stopped believing it will help.

"What's in the bundle?" he asks, because it is easier than saying anything else.

She unwraps a corner. Inside, asleep, is a baby no more than four months old, with a fist in its mouth.

Jian looks at it for a long moment.

"Keep him warm too," he says, and goes up the steps into the smoke before she can see his face.

The guard in the doorway watches him go, the old man in the plain gray tunic with the staff, and a thought passes across his face, a thought Jian has seen on a great many faces in a great many years: he is going to die for this.

Jian does not look back.

* * *

He runs at the second hour.

He has resisted it for as long as he can. But the lower road bends around a ridge of broken stone, and at the bend, the smoke clears, and he sees the whole valley spread out beneath him like a map.

It is not a valley any more. It is a river of pale bodies, flowing north. Thousands. They crowd the road and the terraces and the dry ditches, climbing over each other, a slow dreadful tide, and at the far end of the tide, a long dark line against the horizon: the Valley Wall, and the Sect banners above it, and a thin sparking haze where the arrays are burning.

Eight miles.

He cannot walk through that. Nor can he fight through it. He is a man of a hundred and nineteen years in a body that is failing, and he has perhaps five months, and the number of things left in the world that he cares about could be counted on his fingers.

He counts them anyway.

Wenyuan. Qinghe. Feng. Yue. The thought of Yue's silent face, her small steady hand on the Pebble in the dark. Lan Wen. The wall.

Then he lowers his staff and takes the Core Step.

It is not a leap. It never is. There is a tightening in the lower belly, a pressure, a sense of the world folding over like a sheet of paper in the hands of a patient man, and then he is not where he was. He is two hundred paces down the road, on the far side of a crawler that has not yet noticed him. His boots strike dirt. The staff comes round in a short, vicious arc and takes the beast behind the jaw, and it falls.

One.

He folds again.

Two hundred paces. Three hundred. A stone ridge, a ditch of dead things, a stretch of road so thick with bodies that he has to hop from the back of one to the next. The world blurs. His breath comes in great ragged heaves, and each fold scrapes the Core, a long dry rasp he feels in the roots of his teeth. The gold is going. He can feel it going. A small bright flake of his own substance, every time, torn off and lost.

Eleven, he thinks. Twelve. Thirteen.

At nineteen he stops counting.

* * *

At the Cold Race bridge, a dozen farmers are holding the road.

He hears them before he sees them: the flat chop of scythes, the grunt of effort, a woman's cracked voice calling a rhythm. The bridge is an old stone arch over a brown stream, forty paces long and just wide enough for two carts, and the whole tide has bunched against it. On the near side stand twelve people in field smocks with their sleeves rolled. Their weapons are the tools of a harvest. One man has a hay fork. A gray-haired woman at the center has a sickle in each hand.

They are losing. He can see it in the way they stand, a tight half-circle that shrinks with every minute, and in the three bodies laid neatly by the parapet.

He comes in from the flank. The Core Step puts him in the middle of the bridge, among the crawlers, with nobody behind him, and the staff takes the first beast across the skull before it can turn. He swings again. He does not think. The old art is in his hands without being asked: a short, low, brutal circle, the weight in the heel, the break and the return. A Gnasher rears. He slides under its jaws and lets the staff do the rest.

"Back!" he shouts to the farmers. "Behind me!"

The gray-haired woman looks at him once, takes in the gaunt face, the gray hair, the blood on his chin, and says in a voice like a rusty gate, "I'll be damned. It's the old hermit."

"Madam, I need you to move."

"Not for a hermit." She plants a foot and slashes. A crawler's leg comes off at the joint. "Get on with it, then. We've been at this since dusk."

They hold the bridge together for an hour. He never learns her name. When the last of the rush has broken against the stone and the survivors are thinning out into the fields, she wipes her sickles on her smock, looks at him, and jerks her chin to the north.

"They're all going the wrong way," she says. "Whatever you came to do, do it quick."

"I will."

"And Hermit." She almost smiles. "Eat something."

He crosses the bridge with the farmers' thanks on his back and his hands trembling on the staff. Behind him, three scythes lie across the parapet, and no one has the strength to pick them up.

At the fourth mile, he falls.

It is a small thing, a stone. His heel catches a root, and his knee goes, and he plunges forward into the road with his staff skittering out of his hand. For a moment he lies there with his face in the dirt and the smell of blood in his nose, and the entire tide of the valley rushing by him on either side.

He does not get up at once.

He cannot. His legs have turned to water. His chest is on fire. Each breath is a rope hauled through a narrow pipe, and he coughs, and coughs again, and when he looks at his hand it is red to the wrist.

Fifteen weeks.

He lies there, and reads it. It had been nineteen, when he came out of the fold. Four weeks, spent in an hour, on a road in the dirt. Four weeks of Mei's keeping. Four weeks of the kettle on the fire and the cold porridge in the kitchen and the sound of his mother's cooking-spoon on the rim of the pot. He tries to feel the loss and cannot. He is too tired. It is a number, only, and the number is very small.

It is the price, he thinks. I knew it. I paid it.

He gets his hand under him. He gets a knee under him. There is a crawler six paces away, he sees, a gray-ribbed thing the size of a dog, and it is looking at him with the blank patient attention of its kind. He reaches for the staff and finds it a yard out of reach.

The crawler takes a step.

From the north, a flat clear note: a horn, three blasts, long and short. And an answering sound from the west, the thin high ringing of a bell.

The crawler lifts its head. It listens. Then it turns, slowly, and goes away down the road, toward the tree.

Jian stays on his knees in the dirt, breathing.

Why? he thinks. And then: No. Don't ask.

He crawls to the staff.

There is a roadside shrine a hundred paces on, a small stone box with a clay lamp in it and a faded ribbon, and he gets as far as its lee and sits down with his back to the wall. The smoke goes over his head. He takes out the pouch and shakes a black wax pill into his palm. It is the fourth since the morning. Bell made them. She stood in the infirmary yard with her sleeves rolled and her hands stained green to the wrist, and she did not look at him while she packed the pouch.

They will keep the blood out of your lungs for half a day, she said. They will not keep you alive. I want you to understand that I can't.

I understand.

Then make them good months, Jian. Her voice cracked on it, once, and she turned her face away. That is all I have ever asked of anyone I could not save.

He chews the pill. It is bitter, and oily, and tastes faintly of cloves.

Good months. He tries the words in his mouth. Fifteen weeks, now. A hundred and five days, and a hundred and five mornings, each with a kettle on a hearth. He would like to spend a few of them doing nothing. Sitting in the kitchen while Qinghe shouts at the pot. Letting Feng tell him the same story about the goat. Watching Wenyuan sleep, and Yue draw, and Lin Kuang practice the stance with his tongue stuck out.

He knows he will not.

There is a Wall to hold, and a tree to guard, and a door under the earth that has a child's life behind it. There is the arithmetic of a hundred and five days against nine million sleepers. He does the sum and does not like the answer, and then, because he is Lin Jian, he puts the answer away and stands up.

Later, he promises the shrine, the lamp, the whole bleeding world. When it is done.

It is the oldest lie there is. He tells it with a straight face.

Out on the road, the horn sounds again, three long notes, and he turns his head toward it like a man turning to a voice he knows. Somewhere ahead, past the smoke and the dead, a woman with white eyes is standing on a wall with two hundred guards and a promise. He has not seen her in twelve days. He finds he would very much like to.

* * *

The last three miles he does on foot, and it takes him until noon.

He does not fold again. He cannot afford to. He walks, with the staff in his right hand and his left pressed flat against his ribs, through the final stretch of the lower road, where the crawlers thin and the Sect arrays begin: first the outer wards, a ring of white stone markers each humming faintly, then the second ring, then the broken ground below the Wall where the pupils have been burning the dead for a day and a night. The smoke here is thick and sweet. Pupils in gray-and-white cloaks go past him with stretchers. None of them look up.

A boy of about fourteen, blackened to the elbows, is drawing water from a barrel. He sees Jian, and the cup stops halfway.

"Elder?" His voice cracks. "Elder Lin?"

"I am only Lin Jian," says Jian. "Is Head Han on the Wall?"

"She's at the Gate tower. Sir, you can't—you look—" The boy's eyes go wide. "Sir, you're bleeding."

"Yes."

"I'll fetch a healer."

"Fetch the Head instead. Tell her the keeper has come back."

The boy stares at him. Then he drops the cup, and runs.

Jian walks the last three hundred paces alone.

The Wall rises in front of him like a cliff of dressed stone, forty feet high, banded with black iron and crowned with a rank of banners that hang limp in the smoke. At its foot, in a cleared half-circle, a hundred pupils stand shoulder to shoulder with their backs to him and their spears set against the dark. Beyond them, on the far side of the killing ground, the tide beats against the stone like a sea.

He sees all this. And he sees, a little to the left of the Gate, a tall woman in a plain gray cloak with a staff in her hand and a white bandage round her forehead, who has turned and is staring at him with an expression he has never seen on her face.

Han crosses the distance at a dead run.

She stops three paces off. Her mouth opens, and shuts. Her eyes go over him once, slowly: the stained cuffs, the gray in his hair, the gaunt hollow of his face. And Jian watches her do the sum, because she is quick, and because she has known him for two decades, and because it takes her only a moment.

"How long?" she says. Her voice is very quiet.

"Fifteen weeks. Perhaps sixteen."

Han says nothing for a long moment. A pupil near her wipes his face with a sleeve and pretends not to listen.

"I was told," she says at last, "that you were coming to save us."

"I am coming to try."

"With fifteen weeks."

"With fifteen weeks," Jian agrees. "I did not choose the number. I only choose what to spend it on."

She looks at him a long time. Then, very slowly, as if it hurts her, she bows. It is the full bow, the one the Sect gives to its dead, and the hundred pupils standing behind her see it, and hear the silence, and one by one, without being told, they turn around.

Jian stands in the smoke on the broken ground before the Gate, with blood on his mouth and fifteen weeks in his chest, and a hundred faces looking at him.

He does not know what to say.

"Tell me where the wall is weakest," he says. "I will start there."
